title: When the Favorite Loses
objective: After this level you can explain why a candidate given a 70% chance should still lose about 3 times in 10, and why that doesn't make the forecast wrong.
summary: A 70% favorite should lose about 3 times in 10. If favorites never lost, the forecasts would be too timid. One result can't prove a probability wrong; a long record can.

cards.headline: The forecast gave her a 70% chance. She lost. Was the forecast wrong?
cards.body: Picture an election forecast, with made-up numbers, that makes one candidate a clear favorite. On election night the underdog wins, and everyone says the forecasters blew it. Maybe they did. But one night can't tell you.

cards.headline: 70% for is 30% against
cards.body: A 70% chance of winning is a 30% chance of losing: 30 in every 100 races like this one, or about 3 in 10. As one forecasting guide puts it, a 75% chance means that 25 times out of 100, the opposite is expected to happen. In Level 7's terms, 30% is close to 1 in 3. A 1 in 3 chance is far from rare.

cards.headline: If favorites never lost, that would be the problem
cards.body: Remember calibration from Level 93? Across all the races a forecaster calls at 70%, the favorite should win about 7 in 10 and lose about 3 in 10. If every one of those favorites won, the forecaster wasn't brilliant, just too timid: they should have said higher than 70%. Upsets, in the right amount, are what honest forecasts look like.

cards.fact: One result can't prove a probability right or wrong.
cards.context: Unless a forecast said 0% or 100%, either outcome was allowed. A forecaster is judged over many forecasts, not one night: do their 70% calls come true about 70% of the time? So when a favorite loses, the fair question isn't "Were they wrong?" It's "How often do their 70%s come true?"

questions.prompt: Match each chance with its other side.
questions.explanation: A 70% chance of winning is a 30% chance of losing. A 75% chance means 25 times out of 100 the opposite happens. And 30% is close to 1 in 3, far from rare.

questions.explanation: Divide 100 by N: 1 in 3 is about 33%, the closest to 30%.
